1.pericope_label: Be strong in grace, and commit it to faithful men

schools.summary: Chrysostom says the young sailor at sea is inspired with great confidence if the master of the ship has been preserved in a shipwreck, for he will not consider that it is from his inexperience that he is exposed to the storm, but from the nature of things; and in war the captain who sees his general wounded and recovered again is much encouraged. Thus it produces some consolation to the faithful that the Apostle should have been exposed to great sufferings and not rendered weak by the utmost of them; and had it not been so, he would not have related his sufferings. When Timothy heard that he who possessed so great powers, who had conquered the whole world, is a prisoner and afflicted, yet is not impatient nor discontented upon the desertion of his friends, he, if ever exposed to the same sufferings himself, would not consider that it proceeded from human weakness nor from his being a disciple and inferior to Paul, since his teacher too suffered the like, but that all this happened from the natural course of things. Paul related what had befallen him that he might strengthen Timothy and renew his courage, and shows that this was his reason by adding, thou therefore, my son, be strong in the grace that is in Christ Jesus. What sayest thou, asks Chrysostom: thou hast shaken us with terrors, thou hast told us that thou art in chains, in afflictions, that all have forsaken thee, and, as if thou hadst not suffered anything, nor been abandoned by any, thou addest, thou therefore, my son, be strong? And justly too; for these things were to thy strengthening more than to his. If I, Paul, endure these things, much more oughtest thou to bear them; if the master, much more the disciple. This exhortation he introduces with much affection, calling him son, and not only so, but my son: if thou art a son, imitate thy father; if thou art a son, be strong in consideration of the things which I have said, or rather be strong, not merely from what I have told you, but of God. Be strong in the grace that is in Christ Jesus, that is, through the grace of Christ, that is, stand firmly. Thou knowest the battle, for elsewhere he says, we wrestle not against flesh and blood; and this he says not to depress but to excite them. Be sober therefore and watch, have the grace of the Lord cooperating with thee and aiding thee in thy contest, contribute thy own part with much alacrity and resolution. Of the deposit he says the things are committed to faithful men, not to questioners nor to reasoners, but to faithful; and how faithful? Such as betray not the Gospel they should preach. The things which thou hast heard, he notes, not which thou hast searched out, for faith cometh by hearing, and hearing by the word of God. And wherefore among many witnesses? As if he had said, thou hast not heard in secret, nor apart, but in the presence of many, with all openness of speech. Nor does he say, tell, but commit, as a treasure committed is deposited in safety. But he says not only commit to faithful men, for of what advantage is it that one is faithful, if he is not able to convey his doctrine to others, when he does not indeed betray the faith, but does not render others faithful? The teacher therefore ought to have two qualities, to be both faithful and apt to teach; wherefore he says, who shall be able to teach others also.

Gill says the illative particle therefore shows the connection between this and the preceding chapter, and that the appellation, thou, my son, expresses the apostle's tender affection for Timothy, and is the rather used to engage his attention to the advice he was about to give him. The advice is that, since Timothy had received the true grace of God and unfeigned faith dwelt in him, and since he had such gifts qualifying him for the work of the ministry, and since so good a thing as the glorious Gospel of the blessed God was committed to his trust, and since there were so many who had departed from it and so few that abode by it, he would have him be strong. Of the things heard he says the apostle means the doctrines of the Gospel, the form of sound words, which the Arabic version renders the secrets or mysteries that thou hast heard of me, the mysteries of the grace of God which he had often heard him unfold and explain. Calvin says that as Paul had formerly commanded Timothy to keep by the Spirit that which was committed to him, so now he enjoins him to be strengthened in grace; by this expression he intends to shake off sloth and indifference, for the flesh is so sluggish that even those who are endued with eminent gifts are found to slacken in the midst of their course if they be not frequently aroused. Some will say, of what use is it to exhort a man to be strong in grace, unless free will have something to do in cooperation? He replies that what God demands from us by his word he likewise bestows by his Spirit, so that we are strengthened in the grace which he has given to us; and yet the exhortations are not superfluous, because the Spirit of God, teaching us inwardly, causes that they shall not sound in our ears fruitlessly and to no purpose. Whoever therefore shall acknowledge that the present exhortation could not have been fruitful without the secret power of the Spirit will never support free will by means of it. That the grace is said to be in Christ Jesus is added for two reasons, to show that the grace comes from Christ alone and from no other, and that no Christian will be destitute of it; for since there is one Christ common to all, it follows that all are partakers of his grace, because all who belong to Christ must have it. The kind appellation which Paul employs, Calvin adds, tends much to gain the affections, that the doctrine may more effectually obtain admission into the heart.

Henry says that those who have work to do for God must stir up themselves to do it and strengthen themselves for it, and that being strong in the grace that is in Christ Jesus may be understood in opposition to the weakness of grace: where there is the truth of grace there must be a labouring after the strength of grace, and as our trials increase we have need to grow stronger and stronger in that which is good, our faith stronger, our resolution stronger, our love to God and Christ stronger. Or it may be understood in opposition to our being strong in our own strength: be strong, not confiding in thy own sufficiency, but in the grace that is in Jesus Christ, as it is elsewhere, be strong in the Lord and in the power of his might. When Peter promised rather to die for Christ than to deny him, Henry says, he was strong in his own strength; had he been strong in the grace that is in Christ Jesus, he would have kept his standing better. There is grace in Christ Jesus, for the law was given by Moses, but grace and truth came by Jesus Christ, and there is grace enough in him for all of us; and we must be strong in this grace, not in ourselves, in our own strength, or in the grace we have already received, but in the grace that is in him, and that is the way to be strong in grace. As a father exhorts his son, so does Paul exhort Timothy, with great tenderness and affection. Timothy must count upon sufferings, even unto blood, and therefore he must train up others to succeed him in the ministry of the gospel: he must instruct others and train them up for the ministry, and so commit to them the things which he had heard, and he must also ordain them to the ministry, lodging the gospel as a trust in their hands. Two things he must have an eye to in ordaining ministers, their fidelity or integrity, that they will sincerely aim at the glory of God, the honour of Christ, the welfare of souls and the advancement of the kingdom of the Redeemer among men, and also their ministerial ability, since they must not only be knowing themselves but be able to teach others and be apt to teach. The things Timothy was to commit to others were what he had heard of the apostle among many witnesses; he must not deliver anything besides, and what Paul delivered to him and others he had received of the Lord Jesus Christ. He was to commit them as a trust, as a sacred deposit, which they were to keep and to transmit pure and uncorrupt unto others; those to whom he was to commit these things must be faithful, that is, trusty men, and skilful to teach others; and though men were both faithful and able to teach others, yet these things must be committed to them by Timothy, a minister, a man in office, for none must intrude themselves into the ministry, but must have these things committed to them by those already in that office.

Clarke summarises the chapter as an exhortation to Timothy to constancy, fidelity and courage, to acquit himself as a true soldier of Jesus Christ, and patiently to expect the fruit of his labours. On the word grace he says that though its genuine import is favour, yet it often implies an active principle communicated from God, light directing how to act and power enabling to act according to the light. The things heard of Paul he takes to be those doctrines which the apostle had preached the most publicly and which many persons can attest; but he seems to refer here, Clarke says, to the doctrines delivered to Timothy when, in the presence of many witnesses, he laid his hands upon him, the apostle then giving him the proper form of sound words which he was to teach, and now telling him to commit those truths to faithful men in the same way that they were committed to him, that the truth might be preserved in the Church and holy men appointed successively to preach it. These truths are still continued in the Church, he adds, and still there are faithful men who proclaim them. But where is the uninterrupted apostolical succession? Who can tell? Probably it does not exist on the face of the world; all the pretensions to it by certain Churches are as stupid as they are idle and futile, and he who appeals to this for his authority as a Christian minister had best sit down till he has made it out, and this will be by the next Greek kalends. Wesley says the things are the wholesome doctrine, that commit means before thou leavest Ephesus, and that the faithful men are those who will be able, after thou art gone, to teach others.

Barnes gives an analysis of the whole chapter, that it is made up of various exhortations and encouragements to duty: the apostle exhorts Timothy to be strong in the Christian graces, to commit the great trust which he had received to faithful men, and to endure hardships like a good soldier, referring him to the case of one who goes to war, to one who strives for a crown at the games, and to the husbandman who looks onward for the reward of his labour; then, to encourage patience, to the certainty of the truth of that religion in whose cause he would suffer, to his own case, to the fact that our sufferings here will be crowned with certain glory hereafter, and to the assurance that the Lord Jesus will be faithful to all his promises. On the first verse he says the words thou therefore look back to the fact stated in the previous chapter, that many had turned away from the apostle and forsaken the paths of truth, and that be strong in the grace which is in Christ Jesus means, be strong, relying on the grace which the Lord Jesus only can impart. Of the things heard among many witnesses he says perhaps the apostle refers to a solemn charge which he gave Timothy in the presence of the church when he was ordained, since it is by no means improbable that such a charge was given then to a newly ordained minister as it is now, and on such an occasion the apostle would be likely to state a summary of Christian doctrine and to exhort Timothy to a faithful adherence to it. The same commit thou to faithful men means in the same way as those things have been committed to you, the reference being undoubtedly to ordination to the ministerial office: Timothy was to see that those only were admitted to the ministry who were qualified to understand the truths of religion and to communicate them to others. This is a clear warrant for ministers to set apart others to the same sacred office; it does not prove that the people are not at liberty to choose their own pastor, but only that those in the ministry are to set apart others to the same office with themselves. There is doubtless to be a succession of ministers in the church, Barnes says, but the true line of the succession is to be found in good men who are qualified to teach and who have the Spirit of Christ, and not merely in those who have been ordained. Ellicott says that after the reference to the faithless Asiatics and the true loyal Onesiphorus, with which he interrupted his exhortation, St Paul turns again to Timothy: thou therefore, my son, considering what has taken place, be strong, as though he said, imitate the one loyal follower and make up to me for the faithless conduct of so many false friends. Thou then be strong, but not as men understand strength or firmness; rather be strong in the grace that is in Christ Jesus, that is, in the power of that inward sanctification which enables a man to will and to do according to what God has commanded, which alone proceeds from Christ and which will never be wanting to anyone who is in Christ. Of the things heard he says these have often been understood as referring to the few great fundamental truths rehearsed by the Apostle in the presence of the elders of the congregation on the occasion of Timothy's solemn ordination, so that they would be something of the nature of what is contained in a creed or profession of faith; but it is better to give them a much broader reference and to understand them as comprehending far more than the narrow limits of a profession of faith could possibly contain. The things were no doubt the sum of St Paul's teaching, the general conception of Pauline theology, which Timothy, so long the Apostle's intimate and confidential friend and disciple, was to give out to another generation of believers; it was the theology shrined in such epistles as those once written to the Romans or Ephesians in past years, and these things Timothy had heard again and again in crowded congregations, before Jewish and Christian elders and before assemblies composed of idolaters. The many witnesses, on this interpretation, included Pagans and Jews, the rich and poor, the untaught sinners of the Gentiles and the skilled rabbi trained in the schools of Jerusalem and Alexandria. The faithful men are not men merely who were believers in Jesus Christ, though this of course was intended, but loyal, trusty souls, men who under no temptation would betray the charge committed to them; and they must also possess knowledge and the power of communicating knowledge to others. Although the divine help was to be prayed for and expected in this and all other sacred works, Ellicott notes how St Paul directs that no ordinary human means of securing success must be neglected, his last charge in these Pastoral Letters directing that only those shall be selected as teachers of religion whose earthly gifts were such as fitted them for the discharge of their duties. While there is nothing in this passage to support the theory of an authoritative oral teaching existing from the days of the Apostles in the Church, the words point to the duty of the Christian soldier not only himself to keep unchanged and safe the treasure of the faith as taught by the Apostle, but to hand down the same unimpaired and safe to other hands: the great Christian truths were never allowed to be recklessly handled, and there was a school, so to speak, of Christian theology in the time of St Paul. Some have imagined that these directions were given to Timothy with a view to his leaving Ephesus for Rome to join the imprisoned Apostle, in which event able as well as devoted men should be left in this great centre to carry on the work; but it is far better to understand the charge as given to Timothy as a representative leader of the Church of Christ, and the Apostle's words as addressed to the Church of all times. The runners in the Christian race, he closes, must take good care before they fall out of the course that their torches, still burning, be handed on to the athletes who take their place. Robertson says be strengthened is the present passive imperative, keep on being empowered, keep in touch with the power, and that in the grace that is in Christ Jesus marks where the power is located: Christ is the dynamo for power only when and while we keep in touch with him. From me is as in the first chapter, Paul being Timothy's chief teacher of Christ; among many witnesses uses the preposition in a sense Plutarch has, and Field suggests it is a legal phrase, supported by many witnesses, so that they are not mere spectators but testifiers. Commit thou is the second aorist middle imperative of the verb to deposit, the same metaphor as the deposit of the first chapter, so that it means deposit thou; faithful means trustworthy or reliable, able means capable or qualified, and others also means not necessarily different but others in addition. This, Robertson says, is the way to pass on the torch of the light of the knowledge of God in Christ: Paul taught Timothy who will teach others who will teach still others, an endless chain of teacher-training and gospel propaganda.

debates: Whether the exhortation to be strong in grace leaves anything to free will: Calvin raises the objection himself and answers that what God demands by his word he bestows by his Spirit, so that the exhortation proves nothing for free will, while Clarke defines grace as an active principle communicated from God, light directing how to act and power enabling to act

What the things heard among many witnesses were: Barnes and Clarke take them as the summary of doctrine delivered at Timothy's ordination, something like a creed, while Ellicott deliberately widens them to the whole sum of Pauline theology and says the narrow limits of a profession of faith could not contain them

What among many witnesses means: Robertson follows Field in taking the preposition as a legal phrase, supported by many witnesses, who are testifiers rather than spectators, where Chrysostom takes it as openness of speech, that Timothy heard nothing in secret or apart

Whether the verse establishes an apostolical succession: Clarke denies that any uninterrupted succession exists on the face of the world and calls the pretensions to it idle, Barnes locates the true line in good men qualified to teach who have the Spirit of Christ rather than merely in the ordained, and Ellicott denies that it supports authoritative oral teaching while insisting the deposit be handed down unimpaired
outliers: Chrysostom's two images, the young sailor whose master survived a shipwreck and the captain who sees his general wounded and recovered
Chrysostom's objection put in Paul's mouth, that he shook his readers with terrors and then told them to be strong
Clarke's dismissal of apostolical succession, that whoever appeals to it had best sit down till he has made it out, and this will be by the next Greek kalends
Ellicott's closing image of runners handing on torches still burning to the athletes who take their place
Ellicott's remark that there was a school, so to speak, of Christian theology in the time of St Paul
Henry's use of Peter, who promised to die rather than deny his Lord in his own strength and so failed to keep his standing
Robertson's figure of Christ as the dynamo, giving power only while we keep in touch with him

3.pericope_label: The soldier, the athlete and the husbandman

schools.summary: Gill says that to endure hardness is to endure afflictions, the same word being used elsewhere and properly signifying to suffer evil, and meaning the evil of afflictions, as persecutions of every kind, loss of name and goods, scourging, imprisonment and death itself, for the sake of Christ and the Gospel. Of the soldier he says the man who warreth is one who is a soldier and gives himself up to military service in a literal sense; the Vulgate Latin version, without any authority, adds the words to God, as if the apostle were speaking of a spiritual warfare, whereas he is illustrating a spiritual warfare by a corporeal one. Striving for masteries he takes of the Olympic games, by running, wrestling and leaping; and the husbandman that laboureth he takes of manuring the ground, ploughing, sowing, weeding and reaping. On the charge to consider, Gill says the advice given was to be strong in the grace of Christ, to commit the doctrines of the Gospel to faithful and able men, and to endure hardness for the sake of it, together with the characters Timothy was to bear as a soldier, a runner in a race or a wrestler, and a husbandman, so that he must not expect ease and rest but war, difficulties, toil and labour. He should also consider under what titles Christ was to be regarded: as his General and the Captain of salvation who commanded him, as the righteous Judge who held the prize and crown for which he was running, and as the chief Shepherd who would reward all his labours; and likewise the glorious reward of grace itself, eternal life when he had fought the good fight, the crown of righteousness when he had finished his course, and a crown of glory that fades not away when the chief Shepherd should appear. By putting him upon the consideration of these things, Gill says, the apostle suggests that they were matters of moment and importance.

Clarke says the apostle considers a Christian minister under the notion of a soldier, not so much for his continual conflicts with the world, the devil and the flesh, for these are in a certain sense common to all Christians, but for the hardships and difficulties to which he must be exposed who faithfully preaches the Gospel of Christ. On the entanglement he remarks with Grotius that the legionary soldiers among the Romans were not permitted to engage in husbandry, merchandise, mechanical employments or anything that might be inconsistent with their calling, and that many canons have at different times been made to prevent ecclesiastics from intermeddling with secular employments: he who will preach the Gospel thoroughly, and wishes to give full proof of his ministry, had need to have no other work, but should be wholly in this thing, that his profiting may appear unto all. There are many who sin against this direction, he says: they love the world and labour for it, and are regardless of the souls committed to their charge. But what are they, either in number or guilt, compared to the immense herd of men professing to be Christian ministers, who neither read nor study, and consequently never improve? These are too conscientious to meddle with secular affairs, and yet have no scruple of conscience to while away time, be among the chief in needless self-indulgence, and by their burdensome and monotonous ministry become an incumbrance to the Church. Do you inquire in what sect or party these are to be found? He answers, in all: idle drones, born to consume the produce of the soil, disgrace every department in the Christian Church, and they cannot teach because they will not learn. Of the games he says the word means to contend in the public games, the Olympic or Isthmian games among the Greeks, and refers the reader to his fuller note on First Corinthians; though a man may have conquered, he is not crowned except he strive lawfully, that is, unless he enter according to the rules of the athlete and act as these direct, and no man, however zealous, is to expect the well done, good and faithful servant from Jesus Christ unless he have laboured in the word and doctrine, preached the truth as it is in Jesus, and built up the Church upon him who is its only foundation. The husbandman must first till his ground before he can expect a crop, and must till it according to the proper rules of agriculture, else he cannot have a crop; the combatant must fight and conquer, and fight according to the laws of the contests, before he can be crowned; so the Christian minister must labour in the spiritual vineyard, and labour too under the eye and according to the direction of his Master, before he can expect that crown of righteousness that fadeth not away. On the last verse he says, apply my metaphors and similitudes in a proper manner; and instead of may he give, several manuscripts, versions and fathers have he will give. Consider thou properly, and God will give thee a proper understanding of all things that concern thy own peace and the peace and prosperity of his Church: think as well as read. Wesley says no man that warreth entangleth himself any more than is unavoidable, in the affairs of this life meaning with worldly business or cares, so that minding war only he may please his captain; and he notes that in this and the next verse there is a plain allusion to the Roman law of arms and to that of the Grecian games, since according to the former no soldier was to engage in any civil employment, and according to the latter none could be crowned as conqueror who did not keep strictly to the rules of the game.

Barnes says the apostle supposes that a minister of the gospel might be called to endure such hardships as a soldier is called to endure, and that it is reasonable he should be as ready to do it as a soldier is. Soldiers often endure great privations: taken from their homes and friends, exposed to cold or heat or storms or fatiguing marches, sustained on coarse fare or almost destitute of food, they are often compelled to endure as much as the human frame can bear, and often sink under their burdens and die. If for reward or their country's sake they are willing to do this, the soldier of the cross should be willing to do it for his Saviour's sake and for the good of the human race; hence let no man seek the office of the ministry as a place of ease, and let no one enter it who is not prepared to lead a soldier's life and to welcome hardship and trial as his portion. He would make a bad soldier, Barnes says, who at his enlistment should make it a condition that he be permitted to sleep on a bed of down, and always be well clothed and fed, and never exposed to peril or compelled to pursue a wearisome march; yet do some men not enter the ministry making these the conditions, and would they enter it on any other terms? On the entanglement he says neither the minister nor the soldier is to be encumbered with the affairs of this life, and this is always a condition in becoming a soldier: he gives up his own business during the time for which he is enlisted and devotes himself to the service of his country, as the farmer leaves his plough, the mechanic his shop, the merchant his store, the student his books and the lawyer his brief. He cites Grotius on the rules of war among the Romans, that Roman soldiers were not allowed to marry, or to engage in any husbandry or trade, and were forbidden to act as tutors to any person, or curators to any man's estate, or proctors in the cause of other men, the general principle being that they were excluded from those relations, agencies and engagements which it was thought would divert their minds from that which was to be the sole object of pursuit. So with the ministers of the gospel, he says: it is equally improper for them to entangle themselves with the business of a farm or plantation, with plans of speculation and gain, and with any purpose of worldly aggrandizement. That he may please him who hath chosen him means him who has enlisted him, his great object being to approve himself to him; nowhere else is it so true that the will of one becomes lost in that of another as in the case of the soldier, for in an army it is contemplated that there shall be but one mind, one heart, one purpose, that of the commander. Of the games he says no one could obtain the prize unless he had complied with all the laws of the games and had thus given to those with whom he contended a fair opportunity to succeed, and he quotes the remark that in those contests he who transgressed the rules in the least matter not only failed of the prize, even though the apparent victor, but was sometimes disgraced and punished. On the husbandman he weighs the two constructions: the idea according to the translation in the text is that there is a fitness or propriety that the man who cultivates the earth should enjoy the fruits of his labour, but if this be the meaning it is not easy to see why the apostle introduces it; according to the marginal reading the word first is introduced in connexion with the word labour, so that it is a great law that the husbandman must work before he receives a harvest, and this sense will accord with the purpose of the apostle, which was to remind Timothy that labour must precede reward, that if a man would reap he must sow, and that he could hope for no fruits unless he toiled for them. The point was not that the husbandman would be the first to partake of the fruits, but that he must first labour before he obtained the reward, and thus understood it would be an encouragement to Timothy to persevere while looking onward to the reward; the Greek will bear this construction, Barnes says, though it is not the most obvious one. On the charge to consider he paraphrases: think of the condition of the soldier and the principles on which he is enlisted, think of the aspirant for the crown in the Grecian games, think of the farmer patiently toiling in prospect of the distant harvest, and then go to your work with a similar spirit. When the minister of the gospel thinks of his hardships, of his struggles against an evil world, and of his arduous and constant discouraging toil, let him think of the soldier, of the man who struggles for this world's honours, and of the patient farmer, and be content: how patiently do they bear all, and yet for what inferior rewards. Such are often the discouragements of the ministry, and so prone is the mind to despondency, that we need the help of the Lord to enable us to apply the most obvious considerations and to derive support from the most plain and simple truths and promises. Ellicott says the older authorities do not contain the Greek word rendered thou therefore, and that the word translated endure hardness is in the older authorities compounded with a preposition and better and more literally rendered, take thy share in suffering: Timothy must remember that if he obeys St Paul's voice and with steady earnestness follows his tracks, the very same sufferings which have been the master's guerdon will be the lot of the loyal disciple. He must look on himself as one of the pioneers of the army of the great King, as a tried veteran, as a good soldier of Jesus Christ, prepared for the dangers and trials which in those days awaited such a calling; and then, under three different pictures, the Apostle paints the duties and rewards of a Christian's life. The first picture, of the man engaged on military service, was very familiar to the numerous peoples dwelling under the shadow of the Roman power: the legionary wrapped up in his service, with no thought or care outside the profession of which he was so proud, having nothing to do with buying or selling, with the Forum, or any of the many employments of civil life. So should it be with the earnest and faithful Christian, since paramount and above any earthly considerations must rank his Master's service; the soldier of Christ should never allow himself to be entangled in any earthly business which would interfere with his duty to his own General. Beneath the surface, Ellicott adds, a solemn injunction may be read addressed to those specially engaged in the ministry of the Word, and so the Catholic Church has generally understood this direction as warning her ministers from engaging in secular pursuits, either connected with business or pleasure. The phrase rendered who hath chosen him to be a soldier is more accurately, who enrolled him as a soldier; only those soldiers who with heart and soul devote themselves to their military work win the heart of their commander. The question has been asked, what of St Paul's own example and that of other early Christian teachers such as Aquila, who from time to time pursued the secular calling of tent-makers? The reply, he says, is not difficult: Jewish life in those days contemplated and even desired that its rabbis and teachers should be acquainted with, and even if necessary practise, some handicraft, the well-known Hebrew saying being that he that teacheth not his son a trade teacheth him to be a thief; in the case of these early teachers this occasional practice of an industry or a trade brought them more directly into contact with their Jewish brethren, and it was thus among the Jewish people that the Hebrew rabbi often passed imperceptibly into a Christian teacher. It must also be borne in mind that in St Paul's case, and in the case of the presbyters of the first and second age, especially if missionaries, it was impossible always to ensure subsistence unless by some exertions of their own they maintained themselves; and it was most desirable that these pioneers of Christianity should ever be above all reproach of covetousness, or even of the suspicion that they wished for any earthly thing from their converts. That it was not intended that any such combination of work, at once for the Church and for the world, should be the rule of ecclesiastical order in coming days, Ellicott says the positive and very plain directions of the ninth chapter of First Corinthians are decisive and incapable of being misunderstood. The second picture is of an athlete chosen to represent the professed servant of Christ, one who after long and careful training contends in the public games then so popular, in wrestling or running, in the chariot-racing, or in the hand-to-hand contests; and again this one, as in the case of the soldier, if he aspired to victory and success, must endure hardness. Lawfully means according to the prescribed conditions of the contest: he must submit himself to the strict rules of the theatre where the games are held, and must besides, if he hopes for a prize, go through all the long and severe training and discipline necessary before engaging in such a contest, Galen using the same phrase in the sense of complying with the recognised rules of training as regarding diet. The third picture is painted from every-day life, the husbandman that laboureth, with an emphasis upon that laboureth, being the successful tiller of the ground; it is the enduring, patient, self-sacrificing toil that is rewarded in the affairs of common life, and as in the world, so in religion. The teaching of St Paul in this triple picture, Ellicott says, is that not every soldier wins his commander's applause, but only the veteran who devotes himself heart and soul to his profession; not every athlete wins the crown or prize, but only he who trains with anxious, painful care; not every tiller of the ground gathers the earth's fruits, but only the patient toiler. So must it be in religious life: it is not enough to say we are Christians, or even to wish to be of the brotherhood of Christ, for men must really live the life they say they love. On the last verse he says the older authorities read will give, and that instead of and the Lord the translation should be, for the Lord will give thee understanding in all things. Some difficulty has been found in explaining why Timothy should be so specially charged to consider St Paul's words here: Theophylact suggested it was because the preceding exhortations were in the form of metaphors, so that he spake all things in an enigmatical form; but surely, Ellicott objects, these metaphors were the reverse of obscure and did not seem to need for their comprehension any special enlightenment. If then we refer the words of this verse exclusively to what precedes, it will be best to understand the charge as directing Timothy's attention to the personal application of each of the pictures; it seems, however, that the words, while referring to what he had said, belong also to the far weightier words he was about to write in the next sentence. Robertson says the verb means suffer hardship with me, the old preacher challenging the young one to share hardship with him for Christ; Paul does not hesitate to use this military metaphor, with which he is so familiar, having used it already in First Corinthians and Second Corinthians and First Timothy, and having called Epaphroditus his fellow-soldier as he did Archippus. No soldier on service means no one serving as a soldier; entangleth himself is an old compound meaning to inweave, found in the New Testament only here and in Second Peter; the affairs is an old word for business or occupation, found only here in the New Testament; and of this life has no this in the Greek, the word meaning the course of life rather than existence. Him who enrolled him as a soldier is a literary word found only here in the New Testament. On the games he notes a sharp distinction between the present subjunctive, to engage in a contest in general, and the aorist, to engage in a particular contest, so that the sense is not except he have contended but simply unless he contend, lawfully being an old adverb meaning agreeably to the law; there is one apodosis for two protases, and the victor in the athletic contests was crowned with a garland. The husbandman that laboureth is the toiling tiller of the soil, first meaning as is natural and right, and to partake being an old word meaning to share in. Consider is the present active imperative of the verb to put your mind on, and understanding is comprehension, from the verb to send together, to grasp; this, Robertson says, is a blessed promise that calls for application.

debates: What endure hardness renders: Ellicott and Robertson both take the older compounded reading, take thy share in suffering or suffer hardship with me, making it a personal appeal from the old preacher to the young one, where Gill keeps the general sense of suffering evil and Clarke narrows it to the hardships peculiar to those who faithfully preach

How far the soldier's disentanglement binds ministers: Barnes and Clarke both draw the Roman rules from Grotius and apply them strictly to farms, trade and speculation, Ellicott reports that the Catholic Church has read the verse as barring secular pursuits of business or pleasure, and Wesley qualifies the whole with the words, any more than is unavoidable

Whether Paul's own tentmaking is a counter-example: Ellicott raises the objection himself and answers from Jewish custom, from the impossibility of missionary subsistence, and from the desirability of being above reproach of covetousness, then denies that the combination was ever meant as a rule, citing First Corinthians nine as decisive

What the husbandman verse teaches: Barnes prefers the marginal construction, labouring first must be partaker, so that the law is that work precedes harvest, and grants the Greek will bear it though it is not the most obvious sense, while Ellicott lays the weight on the participle and reads the reward as belonging to the patient toiler

Why the charge to consider stands here: Theophylact, as reported by Ellicott, held it was because the exhortations were enigmatical metaphors, which Ellicott denies, saying the metaphors were the reverse of obscure, and takes the charge to look forward to the weightier words following as well as back
outliers: Barnes's enlistment test, that he would make a bad soldier who made it a condition to sleep on a bed of down and never be exposed to peril
Barnes's report that a transgressor of the rules of the games was sometimes disgraced and punished even when the apparent victor
Clarke's attack on ministers who neither read nor study, idle drones born to consume the produce of the soil, found in every sect and party
Ellicott's Hebrew proverb, that he who teaches not his son a trade teaches him to be a thief
Ellicott's observation that among the Jewish people the Hebrew rabbi often passed imperceptibly into a Christian teacher
Ellicott's note that Galen uses the word lawfully of complying with the recognised rules of training in diet
Robertson's distinction of tense, that the sense is not except he have contended but simply unless he contend

8.pericope_label: Remember Jesus Christ, and the faithful saying

schools.summary: Chrysostom says many of the weaker sort of men give up the effort of faith and do not endure the deferring of their hope: they seek things present and form from these their judgment of the future. When therefore their lot here was death, torments and chains, and yet he says they shall come to eternal life, they would not have believed, but would have said, what sayest thou? When I live, I die, and when I die, I live? Thou promisest nothing on earth, and dost thou give it in heaven? Little things thou dost not bestow, and dost thou offer great things? That none may argue thus, Chrysostom says, Paul places beyond doubt the proof of these things, laying it down beforehand and giving certain signs: for remember, he says, that Jesus Christ was raised from the dead, that is, rose again after death; and now showing the same thing he says, it is a faithful saying, that he who has attained a heavenly life will attain eternal life also. Whence is it faithful? Because, he says, if we be dead with him, we shall also live with him. For say, shall we partake with him in things laborious and painful, and shall we not in things beneficial? But not even a man would act thus; nor, if one had chosen to suffer affliction and death with him, would he refuse to him a share in his rest, if he had attained it. But how are we dead with him? This death he means both of that in the Laver and that in sufferings, for he says, bearing about in the body the dying of the Lord Jesus, and, we are buried with him by baptism into death, and, our old man is crucified with him, and, we have been planted together in the likeness of his death. But he also speaks here of death by trials, and that more especially, for he was also suffering trials when he wrote it; and this is what he says, if we have suffered death on his account, shall we not live on his account? This is not to be doubted. If we suffer, we shall also reign with him: not absolutely, we shall reign, but if we suffer, showing that it is not enough to die once, the blessed man himself having died daily, but that there was need of much patient endurance, and especially Timothy had need of it. For tell me not, he says, of your first sufferings, but that you continue to suffer.

Gill says the words are spoken either as an encouragement to suffer hardness in the cause of Christ, since he who though he was of the seed of David, of the blood royal and heir to his crown, yet suffered and died, and since he rose again from the dead, those who suffer for his sake shall rise also and live and reign with him for ever; or else as a specimen of the form of sound words which Timothy had heard of the apostle, for this with what follows is a summary of them. Christ being of the seed of David according to the flesh is expressive of his incarnation, shows that he was really come in the flesh and was truly man, and that he assumed human nature with all its frailties and infirmities excepting sin, and was, like David, a man of sorrows and acquainted with griefs; it includes his whole life, his righteousness and obedience to the law of works, and points him out as the true Messiah, well known to the Jews by the name of the son of David. Of the sufferings he says Paul was treated as a malefactor, as if guilty of some capital crime, an enemy to the law of Moses, a pestilent fellow, a mover of sedition everywhere and a ringleader of the sect of the Nazarenes, the Ethiopic version rendering it as a thief; and the trouble he suffered was reproaches, persecutions, whipping, beating, stoning and imprisonment. On the elect he says there is a certain number of persons whom God has chosen in Christ from everlasting unto salvation, who shall certainly be saved; for these Jesus Christ suffered and died, and on their account the Gospel is sent, preached and published to the world, for their sakes ministers are fitted and qualified for their work and have their mission and commission to perform it, and suffer what they do in the execution of it; and since it was for the sake of such, whom God had loved and chosen, that the apostle endured all his reproaches, afflictions and persecutions, he was the more cheerful under them. The faithful saying may refer either to what goes before, that all reproaches and sufferings through the ministration of the Gospel are endured for the elect's sake, or to what follows, which being of moment and difficult to be believed, as that death led to life and sufferings were the way to the kingdom, the apostle prefaces in this manner, affirming that it was sure and certain and to be depended on. If we suffer, he says, we suffer with Christ, as all the elect suffered with Christ when he suffered, since they suffered in him the whole penalty of the law and are partakers of the benefits of his sufferings, as peace, pardon, righteousness, redemption and everlasting salvation; and being called by grace and having made a profession of Christ, they suffer shame and reproach, loss of credit and reputation, sometimes loss of goods and corporeal punishment, and even death itself. Of the last clause Gill says the Syriac and Ethiopic versions read, if we believe not him, and that this may be understood either of such as are altogether destitute of faith, who do not believe in Christ at all and particularly do not believe that he will deny those who deny him, but mock and scoff at his coming and at a future judgment, whose unbelief will not make void his faithfulness, since he will abide faithful to his word of threatening; or of true believers, whose faith is sometimes very low as to its exercise on Christ and with reference to their future glory, but Christ is faithful to all his covenant engagements for them, to bring them to glory, and to every word of promise concerning their happiness, and is ever the same in his love to them and in the efficacy of his blood, righteousness and sacrifice.

Henry says that to encourage Timothy in suffering the apostle puts him in mind of the resurrection of Christ, which is the great proof of his divine mission and therefore a great confirmation of the truth of the Christian religion, so that the consideration of it should make us faithful to our Christian profession and should particularly encourage us in suffering for it: let suffering saints remember this, and look to Jesus, the author and finisher of our faith, who for the joy that was set before him endured the cross, despised the shame, and has now sat down at the right hand of the throne of God. The incarnation and resurrection of Jesus Christ, heartily believed and rightly considered, will support a Christian under all sufferings in the present life. Another thing to encourage him in suffering was that he had Paul for an example: Paul was a man who did good and yet suffered as an evil-doer, and let not Timothy the son expect any better treatment than Paul the father; we must not think it strange if those who do well fare ill in this world, and if the best of men meet with the worst of treatment. But this was his comfort, that the word of God was not bound: persecuting powers may silence ministers and restrain them, but they cannot hinder the operation of the word of God upon men's hearts and consciences, which cannot be bound by any human force; and this might encourage Timothy not to be afraid of bonds for the testimony of Jesus, for the word of Christ, which ought to be dearer to him than liberty or life itself, should in the issue suffer nothing by those bonds. Though the preachers of the word are often bound, Henry says, yet the word is never bound. Why Paul suffered cheerfully is that he endured all things for the elect's sake: good ministers may and should encourage themselves in the hardest services and the hardest sufferings with this, that God will certainly bring good to his church and benefit to his elect out of them; and next to the salvation of our own souls we should be willing to do and suffer anything to promote the salvation of the souls of others. The elect are designed to obtain salvation, this salvation is in Christ Jesus as the fountain, the purchaser and the giver of it, and it is accompanied with eternal glory. A third encouragement is the prospect of a future state: those who faithfully adhere to Christ and to his truths and ways, whatever it cost them, will certainly have the advantage of it in another world, for if in conformity to Christ we be dead to this world, its pleasures, profits and honours, we shall go to live with him in a better world; and though we be called out to suffer for him we shall not lose by that, since those who suffer for Christ on earth shall reign with Christ in heaven, as those who suffered with David in his humiliation were preferred with him in his exaltation. It is at our peril if we prove unfaithful to him: if we deny him before man, he will deny us before his Father, and that man must needs be for ever miserable whom Christ disowns at last. This will certainly be the issue whether we believe it or no, for if we believe not, yet he abideth faithful and cannot deny himself: he is faithful to his threatenings, faithful to his promises, and neither one nor the other shall fall to the ground. If we be faithful to Christ he will certainly be faithful to us; if we be false to him, he will be faithful to his threatenings, and cannot recede from any word that he hath spoken, for he is yea and amen, the faithful witness. Our being dead with Christ precedes our living with him and is connected with it, the one being in order to the other, so our suffering for him is the way to reign with him; this is a faithful saying, and may be depended on and ought to be believed. This truth, Henry closes, makes sure the unbeliever's condemnation and the believer's salvation.

Clarke says the apostle seems to say that whatever tribulations or deaths may befall us, let us remember that Jesus Christ, who was slain by the Jews, rose again from the dead, and his resurrection is the proof and pledge of ours: we also shall rise again to a life of glory and blessedness. According to my Gospel he explains by the false teaching of Hymeneus and Philetus, who stated that the resurrection was past already: Paul preached the resurrection from the dead and founded his doctrine on the resurrection and promise of Christ, and this was his Gospel, the other being of a different nature. The mention of suffering trouble as an evil-doer he takes as one of the proofs that this epistle was written while St Paul was a prisoner the second time at Rome, referring to his preface where the point is particularly considered. For the elect's sake he takes of the Gentiles, elected by God's goodness to enjoy every privilege formerly possessed by the Jews, and in addition all the blessings of the Gospel, the salvation of Christ here and eternal glory hereafter. On the faithful saying he says that as surely as Christ rose again from the dead, so surely shall we rise again, and if we die for him we shall surely live again with him; this, says the apostle, is a true doctrine, which is properly the import of the word, and we need not seek, as Bishop Tillotson and many others have done, for some saying of Christ which the apostle is supposed to be here quoting and which he learned from tradition. If we suffer with him, and the clauses that follow, are other parts of the true doctrine which the apostle mentions above; and should we deny the faith and apostatise, he is the same, as true to his threatenings as to his promises, and cannot deny, that is, act contrary to, himself. Wesley says of the seed of David is the one genealogy to attend to; that the word of God is not bound means not hindered in its course; and that Paul, encouraged by this, endured all things, in which we see the spirit of a real Christian, so that one may ask who would not wish to be likeminded, salvation being deliverance from all evil and glory the enjoyment of all good. To deny him, Wesley adds, is to escape suffering for him; and if we believe not means that though some believe not, God will make good all his promises to them that do believe, since he cannot deny himself and his word cannot fail.

Barnes says the sense is rather, remember Jesus Christ, who was raised from the dead: the idea seems not to be, as our translators supposed, that Timothy was to reflect on the fact that he was raised from the dead, but rather that he was to think of the Saviour himself, now raised up from the dead after all the sorrows of this life, and let this encourage him to bear his trials; there is nothing better fitted to enable us to endure the labours and trials of this life than to think of the Saviour. Of the imprisonment he says Paul is treated as if he were a violator of the laws, as if he were one of the worst kind of malefactors. During the apostle's first imprisonment at Rome he was permitted to dwell in his own hired house, though guarded by a soldier and probably chained to him; what his condition was in his second imprisonment, during which this epistle was written, we have no means of knowing with certainty, though it is probable that he was subjected to much more rigid treatment than in the first instance. The tradition is that he and Peter were together in the Mamertine prison at Rome, and the place is still shown in which it is said that they were confined. The Mamertine prisons are of great antiquity: according to Livy they were constructed by Ancus Marcius and enlarged by Servius Tullius; the lower prison is supposed to have been once a quarry and to have been at one time occupied as a granary. These prisons are on the descent of the Capitoline Mount towards the Forum, and consist of two apartments, one over the other, built with large uncemented stones; there is no entrance to either except by a small aperture in the roof, and by a small hole in the upper floor leading to the cell below, without any staircase to either. The upper prison is twenty-seven feet long by twenty wide, and the lower one is elliptical and measures twenty feet by ten; in the lower one is a small spring which is said at Rome to have arisen at the command of Peter to enable him to baptize his keepers, Processus and Martianus, with forty-seven companions whom he converted. No certain reliance can be placed on any part of this tradition, Barnes says, though in itself there is no improbability in supposing that these prisons may have been used for confining Christians, and the apostle Paul among others; and he reports the judgment of Dr Burton that a more horrible place for the confinement of a human being can scarcely be conceived. But the word of God is not bound, he says, is one of Paul's happy turns of thought: the gospel was prospered, and that could not be fettered and imprisoned, but circulated with freedom even when he who was appointed to preach it was in chains; as this was the great matter, his own imprisonment was of comparatively little consequence, for what may befall us is of secondary importance, the grand thing being the triumph of truth on the earth. What the apostle suffers is in the cause of the church, spoken of here as chosen or elected, and their salvation, though they were elected, could not be secured without proper efforts: the meaning is that he was willing to suffer if he might save others, and any one ought to be willing to suffer in order to secure the salvation of the elect, for it was an object for which the Redeemer was willing to lay down his life. That which the apostle was about to say was worthy of entire credence and profound attention, the object being to encourage Timothy to bear trials by the hope of salvation; the words if we be dead with him, we shall also live with him, are a sort of maxim or settled point often referred to in the Bible, and if we suffer we shall also reign with him means that the members will be treated as the Head is, for we become united with him by faith, and if we share his treatment on earth we shall share his triumphs in heaven. Of the last clause Barnes says it cannot mean that if we live in sin he will certainly save us, as if he had made a promise to the elect or formed a purpose to save them whatever their conduct might be; for he has just said that if we deny him he will deny us, and there is no such promise in the Bible and no such purpose has been formed. The promise is that he that is a believer shall be saved, and there is no purpose to save any but such as lead holy lives; the meaning must be that if we are unbelieving and unfaithful, Christ will remain true to his word, and we cannot hope to be saved. He cannot deny himself implies that it would be a denial of his very nature to save those who are unfaithful: he is holy, and how can he save one who is unholy? His very nature is purity, and how can he save one who has no purity? Let no one then suppose that because he is elected he is safe if he lives in sin; the electing purpose of God indeed makes salvation sure, but it is only for those who lead righteous lives, and nothing would be more dishonourable for God than to resolve to save a man that lived habitually in sin. If that were the doctrine of election, Barnes says, it would deserve all the opprobrium that has ever been heaped upon it. Ellicott says the rendering should be, remember Jesus Christ as one raised from the dead, born of the seed of David, since the words of the Greek original, of the seed of David, come after and not before, was raised from the dead. Timothy was to bear in mind two great facts which were to be the foundation stones of his whole life's work, and remembering these in the hour of his greatest trouble he was never to be cast down: that Jesus Christ, for whose sake he suffered, was born of flesh and blood, and yet had risen from the dead. The thought of the Resurrection would always be reminding him of his Master's victory over death and of his present glory; the thought of the Incarnation would ever be whispering to him that the risen and glorified One sprang too, like himself, from mortal flesh and blood. The reason of the Incarnation being expressed in the special manner, born of the seed of David, was to include another truth, that the risen One belonged to the very race specified in those prophets so revered by Timothy and the chosen people as the race from which should spring the Messiah, as in Jeremiah's promise of a righteous Branch raised unto David. To raise the fainting heart of his much-tried disciple in this hour of discouragement, and to supply a ground of confidence to yet unborn Christians who in their day would be tried as Timothy was then, was the Apostle's first purpose in pressing these thoughts on his son in the faith; but in the background, no doubt, there lay another purpose, since these great comforting truths were to be maintained and taught in the presence of those false teachers who were ever ready to explain away or even to deny the beginning and the end of the Son of God's life and ministry on earth. Of the phrase according to my gospel, which occurs frequently in St Paul's Epistles and with slight variations elsewhere, Ellicott quotes Jerome's remark that as often as St Paul writes according to my Gospel he refers to the volume of Luke, and says that although received with reserve by many expositors, considering the weighty traditional evidence we possess of St Luke's Gospel being in reality written by St Paul, it appears on the whole substantially correct. On the sufferings he says St Paul bids Timothy take courage by thinking of the brave, patient example he was setting him in his Roman prison, undaunted and full of hope, and that the word rendered evil doer is better rendered as a malefactor, the same word used in St Luke's Gospel for the two thieves crucified with Jesus Christ: a prisoner in chains, and expecting death, and yet he still could write and pray and speak from his narrow prison, so that surely his disciple, still free, ought to work on with undiminished spirit and zeal. Of the elect he says the rendering should be, for this cause I endure all things, that the word of God may be widely spread and disseminated, and that he does it for those whom God has been pleased to choose as his people and for those who are yet to be brought into the one fold; the endurance contributed to this both as an example to many, not only to the generation then living but to countless men and women yet unborn, and through such writings as this Epistle. The question has often been asked whether those elect were, when he wrote, believers, and Ellicott answers with some certainty that they include both believers and unbelievers, the first being built up by the contemplation of the steadfastness of St Paul under suffering, the second won to the faith by the arguments and exhortations which the brave old man ceaselessly spoke or wrote down in prison just as when free. Of the faithful saying he says that many have supposed, from the rhythmical character of the clauses, that it was taken from some most ancient Christian hymns composed and used in the very earliest days of the faith; but whether or no this be the case, there is high probability that the words formed part of a liturgy in common use in the days of Timothy, and if not a hymn, which seems on the whole the most likely supposition, we can well conceive them as part of the tapestry of a primitive Christian liturgy, woven in like the introductory sentences in our morning and evening prayer, or like the comfortable words of the Communion Service. If we be dead with him is more accurately, if we died with him, and is well explained by the words, I die daily; the Apostle died when he embraced the lot of daily death, and the meaning is further illustrated where we read how St Paul and his companions were always bearing about in the body the dying of the Lord Jesus. The word rendered suffer would be better translated, if we endure, that is, if we bravely bear up against sufferings for his sake; and if we do this in this life we shall in the life to come reign with him, more than merely live with him, since we shall even be kings with him, a promise which gives a strangely glorious hope concerning the active and personal work with which Christ's redeemed will be entrusted in the ages of eternity. But there is another side: while to the faithful he will grant to sit down with him on his throne, the faithless will have no share in the glories of the life to come, and these grave warnings are apparently addressed rather to unfaithful members of the outward and visible Church than to the Pagan world who have never known Christ; the words, he also will deny us, imply something of an expectation on our part that he would recognise us as friends, and are evidently an echo of the Lord's own sad reply to those many who will say to him in that day, Lord, Lord, have we not prophesied in thy name. Of the last clause Ellicott says the rendering should be, if we are faithless, that is, untrue to the vows of our Christian profession, the faithlessness implying more than mere unbelief in any of the fundamental doctrines of the faith. Those who have understood these words as containing soothing, comforting voices for the sinner, for the faithless Christian who has left his first love, are gravely mistaken: the passage is one of distinct severity, and may even be termed one of the sternest in the Book of Life, for it tells how it is impossible even for the pitiful Redeemer to forgive in the future life. He cannot deny himself, that is, cannot treat the faithless as though he were faithful, cannot act as though faithfulness and faithlessness were one and the same thing; the Christian teacher, such as Timothy, and the members of his flock likewise, must remember that, sure and certain as are the promises of glory and happiness to those who love the Lord and try to live his life, so surely will fall the chastisement on all who are faithless and untrue. Robertson says risen from the dead is a perfect passive participle, still risen as the perfect tense shows, and a predicate accusative, so that the sense is, remember Jesus Christ as risen from the dead; this is the cardinal fact about Christ that proves his claim to be the Messiah, the Son of God. Of the seed of David marks the humanity of Christ, and according to my gospel is Paul's very phrase elsewhere, meaning not a written gospel but my message. Wherein means in my gospel; I suffer hardship is an old compound meaning I suffer evil; unto bonds means up to bonds, a common experience with Paul; as a malefactor is an old compound meaning doer of evil, found in the New Testament only here and in Luke of the robbers, and was one of the charges made against Paul. Is not bound is the perfect passive of an old verb: I am bound with a chain, Robertson says, but no fetters are on the word of God. For the elect's sake means because of the elect, for whom Paul suffered so much; the purpose clause means they as well as I; and the salvation is the final salvation with eternal glory, a phrase found only here and in First Peter. Of the faithful saying he says it refers to what follows, though it can refer to the preceding, and that it is possible that from here to the end of the thirteenth verse we have the fragment of an early hymn: there are four conditions in these verses, all of the first class, assumed to be true, and he notes the compounds meaning we died with, we shall live with, and we shall reign with. The verb to deny is an old word, common in the Gospels in the sayings of Jesus and used of Peter, and common in the Pastorals; here in the thirteenth verse it has the notion of proving false to oneself, a thing that Christ cannot do.

debates: Whether the last clause comforts or threatens: Wesley takes it as assurance that though some believe not God will keep his promises to those who do, while Ellicott calls the comforting reading a grave mistake and the passage one of the sternest in the Book of Life, Barnes turns it against any doctrine of election that would save a man living in sin, and Clarke reads it as making Christ as true to his threatenings as to his promises; Gill and Henry hold both senses together

Whether the faithful saying is a quotation: Ellicott judges it most likely an ancient Christian hymn, or at least part of a liturgy in common use, and Robertson allows the hymn fragment with its four first-class conditions, where Clarke denies there is anything to look for and rebukes Tillotson and others for hunting a saying of Christ preserved by tradition

How to construe the opening charge: Ellicott reorders the Greek to give, remember Jesus Christ as one raised from the dead, born of the seed of David, making two facts of it, Resurrection and Incarnation, where Barnes shifts the emphasis from the fact of the rising to the person of the Saviour himself

Who the elect are here: Gill takes them as the fixed number chosen in Christ from everlasting, Clarke as the Gentiles elected to the privileges formerly possessed by the Jews, Ellicott as including both believers and unbelievers yet to be brought into the fold, and Barnes insists their salvation could not be secured without proper efforts
outliers: Barnes's excursus on the Mamertine prison, its quarry, its roof aperture and its spring said to have risen at Peter's command
Barnes's judgment that the word of God not being bound is one of Paul's happy turns of thought
Chrysostom's imagined objector asking, when I live, I die, and when I die, I live?
Chrysostom's note that the promise is not absolutely that we shall reign but only if we suffer, since Paul himself died daily
Clarke's link between according to my gospel and the error of Hymeneus and Philetus that the resurrection was past already
Ellicott's citation of Jerome, that whenever Paul writes according to my Gospel he means the volume of Luke
Ellicott's suggestion that the saying was woven into the liturgy like the comfortable words of the Communion Service

14.pericope_label: Rightly dividing the word, and the gangrene of error

schools.summary: Gill says the charge to put them in remembrance means either Timothy's hearers, or those to whom he was to commit the things he had heard of the apostle, who must expect to suffer afflictions and endure hardships for the sake of Christ and his Gospel, so that to remind them of the above sayings might be of use and comfort to them; he notes that the clause is wanting in the Arabic version. To study to show oneself approved unto God is not to please men, for such as study to please men are not the servants of Christ, and those approved to and by men are sometimes disapproved by God and Christ; it is rather to show all fidelity and uprightness, speaking out the Gospel openly and freely, with all sincerity, as in the sight of God. The ministry of false teachers, he says, is mere babbling, a voice and nothing else, as the man said of his nightingale: a sound of words but no solid matter in them, great swelling words of vanity, like large bubbles of water, which look big and make a great noise but have nothing in them, containing nothing but vain, empty, idle and trifling stuff, unprofitable and unedifying, and indeed profane, contrary to the nature and perfections of God and not agreeable to the doctrine which is according to godliness; and being palmed upon the Holy Scriptures, it is a profanation of them. All such wicked and empty prate is to be shunned, avoided, discouraged, refused and rejected, and as much as can be a stop should be put to it, both by ministers and by hearers of the word. Of the word that eats he says it is a gangrene, which gnaws and feeds upon the flesh, inflames and mortifies as it goes, spreads swiftly and endangers the whole body, and is therefore to be speedily noticed and stopped; it is better rendered gangrene, as in the marginal reading, than cancer. Of Hymenaeus and Philetus he says they fell from the truth, wandered and departed from it, did not keep to the Scriptures of truth but deviated from them, missed the mark and went astray into gross errors, rejecting the Gospel, the word of truth, in general and in this particular.

Henry says that, having encouraged Timothy to suffer, the apostle comes next to direct him in his work: he must make it his business to edify those under his charge and put them in remembrance of the things they already know, for this is the work of ministers, not to tell people what they never knew before but to put them in mind of what they do know, charging them that they strive not about words. Those that are disposed to strive, he observes, commonly strive about matters of very small moment, and strifes of words are very destructive to the things of God. If people did but consider of how little use most of the controversies in religion are, they would not be so zealous in their strifes of words, to the subverting of the hearers, drawing them away from the great things of God and occasioning unchristian heats and animosities by which truth is often in danger of being lost. People are very prone to strive about words, Henry says, and such strifes never answer any other end than to shake some and subvert others; they are not only useless but very hurtful, and therefore ministers are to charge the people that they do not strive about words, and they are most likely to be regarded when they charge them before the Lord, that is, in his name and from his word, producing their warrant for what they say.

Clarke says that words, not things, have been a most fruitful source of contention in the Christian world, and that among religious people the principal cause of animosity has arisen from the different manner of apprehending the same term, while in essence both meant the same thing; all preachers and divines should therefore be very careful, both in speaking and writing, to explain the terms they use, and never employ them in any sense but that in which they have explained them. To study to show oneself approved unto God is to endeavour so to cultivate and improve the heart and mind that one may not be a reproach to him from whom one professes to receive one's commission. On rightly dividing the word of truth he says it is generally supposed that the apostle alludes to the care taken to divide the sacrifices under the law, the priests studying, in dividing the victim down the spine, to do it so scrupulously that one half of the spinal marrow should be found on each side of the backbone; but probably nothing was much farther from the apostle's thoughts than this view, which is now commonly taken of the subject. Indeed this scrupulous dividing does not appear to have been any original ordinance among the Jews, and though much stress was laid upon it in later times, from the beginning it was not so. The Greek word signifies, first, simply to cut straight or to rectify, and secondly, to walk in the right way, being thus used by Gregory Nazianzen, who in one of his orations opposes it to walking in a bad way, just as related compounds signify to walk in a new way and to walk in a straight way. Therefore by rightly dividing the word of truth we are to understand the minister's continuing in the true doctrine and teaching that to every person, and, according to our Lord's simile, giving each his portion of meat in due season: milk to babes, strong meat to the full grown, comfort to the disconsolate, reproof to the irregular and careless; in a word, finding out the necessities of his hearers and preaching so as to meet those necessities. Profane and vain babblings he takes as the character the apostle gives of the preaching of the false teachers, since whatever was not agreeable to the doctrine of truth was in the sight of God empty and profane babbling, engendering nothing but ungodliness and daily increasing in it. Their word eating as a gangrene he explains as a mortification in the flesh, where the circulation is entirely stopped and putrefaction takes place, which continues to corrupt all the circumjacent flesh, spreading more and more till death takes place, unless stopped by a timely and judicious application of medicine; such is the influence of false doctrine, which fixes its mortal seed in the soul, and this continues to corrupt and assimilate everything to itself till, if not prevented by a timely application of the word of life under the direction of the heavenly Physician, it terminates in the bitter pains of an eternal death, and to such a gangrene the apostle compares the corrupt doctrines of Hymeneus and Philetus. Those men had the truth, he says, but erred or wandered from it, saying the resurrection was already past, and thus denying the resurrection of the body and by consequence future rewards and punishments, which necessarily sapped the foundation of all religion. Wesley says the charge is to remind those who are under Timothy's care, and exclaims how many unnecessary things are thus unprofitably, nay hurtfully, contended for. A workman that needeth not to be ashamed means ashamed either of unfaithfulness or of unskilfulness; and rightly dividing the word of truth means duly explaining and applying the whole scripture, so as to give each hearer his due portion, since they that give one part of the gospel to all, the promises and comforts to unawakened, hardened, scoffing men, have real need to be ashamed. Their word, he adds, if they go on, will be mischievous as well as vain, and will eat as a gangrene; and saying the resurrection is already past is perhaps asserting that it is only the spiritual passing from death unto life.

Barnes says these great principles in regard to the kingdom of Christ would be as useful to others as they were for Timothy, and that charging them before the Lord implies that it was a very important matter. To study to show oneself approved unto God is to give diligence, or to make an effort so to discharge the duties of the ministerial office as to meet the divine approbation: the object of the ministry is not to please men, and such doctrines should be preached, such plans formed and such a manner of life pursued as God will approve, which demands study and care, for there are many temptations to the opposite course. Of the babblings he says their tendency is to alienate the soul from God and to lead to impiety, so that such kinds of disputation are not merely a waste of time but productive of positive mischief: a man fond of contention in religious things is seldom one who has much love for the practical duties of piety, or any very deep sense of the distinction between right and wrong; you will not usually look for him in the place of prayer, nor can you expect his aid in the conversion of sinners, nor will you find that he has any very strict views of religious obligation. The word rendered will eat as doth a canker occurs nowhere else in the New Testament and is derived from a verb meaning to devour or corrode, meaning gangrene or mortification, the death of a part, spreading unless arrested by degrees over the whole body; the words rendered will eat mean will have nutriment, that is, will spread over and consume the healthful parts, so that it will not merely destroy the parts immediately affected but will extend into the surrounding healthy parts and destroy them also. So it is with erroneous doctrines, Barnes says: they will not merely eat out the truth in the particular matter to which they refer, but will spread over and corrupt other truths, since the doctrines of religion are closely connected and dependent on each other. To what extent Hymenaeus and Philetus erred is unknown, and Paul mentions only one point, that pertaining to the resurrection, but says that this was like a gangrene and would certainly, unless checked, destroy all the other doctrines of religion: no man can safely hold a single error, any more than he can safely have one part of his body in a state of mortification. It is not known in what form they held this opinion; it may have been, as Augustine supposes, that they taught there was no resurrection but that which occurs in the soul when it is recovered from the death of sin and made to live anew, or it may be that they held that those who had died had experienced all the resurrection they ever would, by passing into another state and receiving at death a spiritual body fitted to their mode of being. Ellicott says a new division of the Epistle begins with the fourteenth verse: St Paul has been urging Timothy to be strong in endurance, to bear trouble and suffering with brave patience, and now proceeds to charge him respecting the special work he has to do, dealing first with his duties as a teacher of truth brought face to face with teachers of error.
