Timothy and those in his position were to show themselves approved unto God by turning others, over whom they possessed influence, from the pursuit of vain and unprofitable things; then their work would be the work of workmen tested by trial and found to have stood the test, and Ellicott compares the passage in First Corinthians where the final testing of the work done by God's workmen is spoken of in very clear, heart-searching language, St Paul's own words there being evidently in his mind when he wrote this direction. Rightly dividing the word of truth is better rendered rightly laying out the word of truth, since the Greek word literally signifies cutting a straight line; it seems most correct to regard it as a metaphor from laying out a road, as the word is so used in the Greek of Proverbs, or drawing a furrow, the merit of which consists in the straightness with which the work of cutting or laying out is performed, the word of truth being as it were a road which is to be laid out straightly and truly. To affirm, with Alford and Huther-Meyer, that the notion of cutting had been gradually lost, and that the word already in the time of St Paul signified simply to manage rightly, or to treat truthfully without falsifying, and that the exact opposite is to corrupt or adulterate the word of God, seems to Ellicott premature. In the third century Clement of Alexandria certainly uses the word in a sense in which the idea of cutting has been lost, when he writes the noun as an equivalent for orthodoxy; and it is not improbable, Ellicott suggests, that the use of the word here by St Paul gave it a fresh starting-point, and that gradually the original meaning passed out of sight. The word rendered shun is a strong one, signifying literally to make a circuit so as to avoid, or, as Alford paraphrases it, the meaning seems to come from a number of persons falling back from an object of fear or loathing and standing at a distance round it. The tendency of these useless discussions and idle disputes is to lead men into vain and profitless speculations, which end too often, as in the case of Hymenaeus and Philetus, in the most fatal doctrinal error. Their word eating as doth a canker is better rendered, as in the margin, as doth a gangrene, the usual rendering of the various English versions; cancer, which is adopted also by Luther, fails to express the terrible and deathly nature of the word of these false teachers, since the life of the sufferer afflicted with cancer may be prolonged for many years, whereas a few hours is sufficient to put a term to the life of the patient attacked with gangrene, unless the limb affected be at once cut away. To translate this Greek word here by cancer, Ellicott says, is to water down the original, in which St Paul expresses his dread of the fatal influence of the words of these teachers on the lives of many of the flock of Christ; and he quotes Jerome to the effect that a perverse doctrine, beginning with one, at the commencement scarcely finds two or three listeners. Of the error itself he says the resurrection of the body, grounded upon the Lord's own words, was one of the articles of the Christian faith upon which St Paul especially loved to dwell, as in his words before Felix, and that with this resurrection of the body St Paul taught men that the future state of rewards and punishments was intimately bound up, the soul being clothed with a body of glory or with a body of shame according to the deeds done in the flesh. This doctrine appears in very early times to have been questioned by some in the Christian community, since then, as now, the thought was repugnant to the shrinking soul of man that the body in which he lived and sinned would rise again. Robertson says the verb meaning to strive about words was apparently coined by Paul from the noun used in First Timothy, a back formation in that case, and that a mere war of words displeases Paul; the word rendered useful is a late and rare one found only here in the New Testament, and the word rendered to the subverting is an old one from a verb meaning to turn down or over, found only here, giving the sense, because of the overthrow. Give diligence is the first aorist active imperative of an old word; approved unto God is an old adjective in the predicate accusative; a workman that needeth not to be ashamed is a late double compound verbal adjective found in Josephus and here alone. Handling aright is the present active participle of a late and rare compound meaning cutting straight, found only here in the New Testament, occurring in Proverbs for making straight paths, with which he compares the phrase in Hebrews and the description of the Christian faith as the Way in Acts; Theodoret explains it to mean ploughing a straight furrow, Parry argues that the metaphor is the stone mason cutting the stones straight, since the words for cutting and straight are so used, and Robertson asks, since Paul was a tent-maker and knew how to cut straight the rough camel-hair cloth, why not let that be the metaphor, certainly plenty of exegesis being crooked enough to call for careful cutting to set it straight. Shun and babblings he refers to Titus and First Timothy; will proceed is the future active of a verb meaning will cut forward. Will eat is literally will have pasturage or increase, from an old word meaning to pasture, found in the New Testament only here and in John; gangrene is a late word used by medical writers and Plutarch, only here in the New Testament, from a verb meaning to gnaw or eat, an eating, spreading disease. Hymenaeus, he adds, is probably the one mentioned in First Timothy, and nothing is known of Philetus. Have erred means missed the mark, and the saying that the resurrection is past already is a second perfect active infinitive in indirect assertion with the accusative of general reference.

debates: What rightly dividing pictures: Clarke reports and rejects the common view that it alludes to the priests dividing the sacrificial victim down the spine, saying nothing was farther from the apostle's thoughts and that the practice was not an original Jewish ordinance; Ellicott takes it of laying out a road or drawing a furrow; Robertson canvasses Theodoret's furrow, Parry's stone mason, and his own suggestion of the tent-maker cutting camel-hair cloth straight

Whether the sense of cutting was still alive in the word: Ellicott calls it premature to hold with Alford and Huther-Meyer that by Paul's time it meant simply to manage rightly, and grants only that Clement of Alexandria in the third century used the noun for orthodoxy with the cutting gone, suggesting Paul's own use gave the word a fresh start

Whether the word is cancer or gangrene: Ellicott argues from the pace of the two diseases that cancer waters down the original, since a cancer sufferer may live for years where gangrene kills in hours unless the limb is cut away, and Gill agrees the marginal reading is better

What Hymenaeus and Philetus taught: Barnes admits it is unknown, offering Augustine's supposition of a resurrection of the soul from the death of sin, or a spiritual body received at death; Wesley guesses the spiritual passing from death unto life; Ellicott treats it as the denial of an article grounded on the Lord's own words
outliers: Barnes's rule that no man can safely hold a single error, any more than he can safely have one part of his body in a state of mortification
Barnes's portrait of the contentious man, whom you will not usually look for in the place of prayer
Clarke's diagnosis that animosity springs from apprehending the same term differently while both mean the same thing
Gill's figure of the false teachers' ministry as a voice and nothing else, as the man said of his nightingale
Robertson's tent-maker metaphor, that plenty of exegesis is crooked enough to call for careful cutting
Wesley's rebuke of those who give the promises and comforts to unawakened, hardened, scoffing men
The strong word for shun, which Alford derives from persons falling back from an object of loathing and standing at a distance round it

19.pericope_label: The seal on the foundation, and vessels in a great house

schools.summary: Chrysostom says many men are still even now perplexed to account for the fact that the wicked are suffered to remain and are not yet destroyed; various reasons may doubtless be assigned for this, as that they may be converted, or that by their punishment they may be made an example to the multitude. But Paul here mentions a similar case, saying that in a great house there are not only vessels of gold and silver but also of wood and earth, showing by this that as in a great house it is likely there should be a great difference of vessels, so here also in the whole world; for he speaks not of the Church only, but of the world at large. Think not, Chrysostom charges his hearers, that he means it of the Church.

Gill says that the faith which is the faith of God's elect is of the operation of God and the gift of his grace, of which Christ is the author and finisher, and is firm and immovable as a foundation: it is solid and substantial, the substance of things hoped for, permanent and abiding, standing sure because supported by the power of God and the prevalent mediation of Jesus Christ, so that it cannot be overthrown by false teachers, though an historical faith, or the faith of temporary believers, may be. Or the doctrine of the resurrection of the dead may be meant, which was said to be past by the false teachers, and which is a fundamental doctrine of the Gospel, without which the preaching of it is vain and faith is vain, a doctrine of God and of pure revelation, to be effected by his power. Of the great house he says the simile is used to show that it need not seem strange, nor be distressing to anyone's mind, that men of such wicked principles and practices should be in the church of God, since in every great house or palace, the house of a nobleman or the palace of a king, there is a variety of vessels of different matter and for different uses, some of them mean, despicable and dishonourable; and so it is in the church of God. By this great house, Gill says expressly, is not meant the world, as some think, though that is a house built by God, who built all things, and is a very large one. If a man purge himself from these means that if a man clears himself and keeps himself clear from such men as Hymenaeus and Philetus, who are comparable to wooden and earthen vessels and are dishonourable ones, shunning their defiling company and polluting principles, keeping clear of their heresies, not carried away with the errors of these wicked men nor drawn aside by them into immoral practices, but standing fast in the faith and departing from iniquity.

Henry says we may comfort ourselves, in reference to the little errors and heresies that both infect and infest the church and do mischief, with this: that the unbelief of men cannot make the promise of God of no effect, for though the faith of some particular persons be overthrown, yet the foundation of God standeth sure, and it is not possible that they should deceive the elect. Or it may be meant of the truth itself which they impugn, since all the attacks which the powers of darkness have made upon the doctrine of Christ cannot shake it: it stands firm and weathers all the storms which have been raised against it. The prophets and apostles, that is, the doctrines of the Old and New Testament, are still firm; and they have a seal with two mottoes upon it, one on the one side and the other on the other, as is usual in a broad seal.

Clarke says the word for foundation signifies literally a foundation, and especially the foundation of a building, and metaphorically the building itself, often a noble mansion or palace; in this place the apostle compares the religion of Christ to a great or noble mansion, and as this religion is founded on the authority and power of the Almighty it necessarily must stand sure and be permanent. This house has an inscription on it, for so the word seal is frequently understood, and this is evidently an allusion to the ancient temples: above the door of the temple of Delphi there was the Greek word meaning thou art, on which Plutarch has written an express treatise; in many of the Mohammedan mosques the walls are covered with inscriptions, ordinarily sentences taken from the Koran relative to the majesty of God or the nature of his worship; and there was an inscription on the mitre of the high priest among the Jews, Holiness to the Lord. This inscription may here be represented as made with the seal of God, for he stamps this on all things belonging to himself and his worship. But some suppose the word here signifies a contract or covenant by which two parties are bound to fulfil certain conditions and duties, the obligation to which each takes on him by sealing the instrument with his seal; and among the Asiatics these seals have scarcely ever any image or figure on them, but always some very expressive inscription. Clarke says he has seen many of these, and that several of them are before him as he writes; the twofold inscription, one on the seal of each party, may be here alluded to, that on God's seal being, the Lord approveth of them that are his, and that on the seal of his followers being, let every one who nameth the name of the Lord depart from iniquity, so that each has his peculiar inscription. Lord, instead of Christ, is the reading of almost all the manuscripts of importance and the principal versions; and the Lord knoweth means approves, watches over and provides for them that are his true followers. Of the great house he says the apostle carries on the allusion introduced in the preceding verse: as the foundation of God refers to God's building, the whole system of Christianity, so here the great house is to be understood of the same, and the different kinds of vessels mean the different teachers as well as the different kinds of members; in the sacred house at Ephesus there were vessels of gold and silver, eminent, holy, sincere and useful teachers and members, and also vessels of wood and of earth, false and heretical teachers such as Hymeneus and Philetus and their followers. He that takes heed to his ways and to his doctrines, and walks with God, will separate himself not only from all false doctrine but from all wicked men, and thus be sanctified and proper to be employed by the Master in every good word and work. The apostle, Clarke adds, has not made the application of these different similes, and it is very difficult to tell what he means. Wesley says the foundation of God is his truth and faithfulness, and that it standeth fast and can never be overthrown, being as it were sealed with a seal which has an inscription on each side: on the one, the Lord knoweth those that are his; on the other, let every one who nameth the name of the Lord, as his Lord, depart from iniquity. Indeed, he says, they only are his who depart from iniquity, and to all others he will say, I know you not. In a great house, such as the church, it is not strange that there are not only vessels of gold and silver designed for honourable uses, but also of wood and of earth for less honourable purposes; yet a vessel even of gold may be put to the vilest use, though it was not the design of him that made it. To purge oneself from these is to purge oneself from vessels of dishonour, so as to have no fellowship with them.

Barnes says the meaning is that though some had been turned away by the arts of these errorists, yet the foundation of the church which God had laid remained firm, and as long as this foundation remained firm there was no reason to be troubled from the few instances of apostasy which had occurred; it is not uncommon, he notes, to compare the church to a building erected on a solid foundation. Having this seal means rather a seal with this inscription, the word seal being used sometimes to denote the instrument by which an impression is made and sometimes the impression or inscription itself. Of the great house he says the idea is that the church is a large edifice, and that in such a building we are not to expect entire uniformity in all the articles which it contains: we are not to expect to find all the articles of furniture alike, or all made of the same material, since variety in form and use and material is necessary in furnishing such a house, some vessels being for the more honourable uses, as drinking vessels and vessels to contain costly viands, and some for the less honourable purposes connected with cooking. If a man purge himself from these refers to the persons represented by the vessels of wood and of earth, and the idea is that if one would preserve himself from the corrupting influence of such men he would be fitted to be a vessel of honour, employed in the most useful and honourable service in the cause of his Master, and fit to be employed by the Lord Jesus in promoting his work on earth. Ellicott says the rendering should be, nevertheless God's firm foundation standeth: though some may be shaken in faith by the unhappy teaching above referred to, yet assuredly God's firm foundation stands unshaken. The firm foundation laid by God is the Church of Christ, so termed because it is the ground-storey of the glorious Temple of the future; in other words the Church of Christ is here considered as the foundation of a far grander building which in the fulness of time will rest upon its massive work, and this ground-storey, the corner-stone of which is Christ, standeth age after age in spite of any efforts made to destroy or even to shake it. The term foundation, here used for the Church of God on earth, is remarkable and points to a great truth: that after all this life is but a beginning, and that his Church here is but a foundation, only the first and early storey of that glorious Church the Divine Architect has planned and will complete in heaven. It was a custom dating back from the very earliest times to inscribe upon a building or monument an inscription which told of its origin and purpose: in some cases, as in the oldest monuments of Egypt, the engraved writing told the name of the royal or priestly builder, and in the Revelation we read how in the wall of the City of God there were twelve foundations bearing the names of the Twelve Apostles of the Lamb. On this foundation storey was carved a legible inscription in two sentences, the one telling of comfort and hope, reminding men God would ever know his own, the other telling of duty, reminding men that God's own had no share in unrighteousness; it is called a seal here instead of an inscription, for a seal best conveys the idea of the solemn binding character of the writing, and the Jew was especially accustomed to see the words and promises of his God written or graven on his doorposts and on his gates, as Job would have his most solemn declaration of faith graven or sealed on a rock for ever. The first sentence was probably a memory of Numbers, but the thought goes far deeper: God's own people, as they read the words graven with an iron pen and with lead for ever, are ever reminded of their deepest, highest, truest comfort, and the words may be paraphrased, he knows his own because he loves them, and never will he cease to know them but will keep them for ever. The thought and words of the second sentence are from the Old Testament, expressed in a wider and more general form in Isaiah's command to depart and touch no unclean thing, being clean that bear the vessels of the Lord; and naming the name of Jesus must be understood in the sense of the confession that Jesus is Lord, so that this sentence signifies that no man confessing with the heart that Jesus is Lord can commit iniquity deliberately, the two things being utterly incompatible. Iniquity here includes the teaching of those false men above alluded to, since their teaching led away from the truth and resulted in a lax and evil way of life. Of the great house he says the Apostle goes on with the same thought of the Church of God on earth but changes the imagery, answering as it were a question which would naturally occur to Timothy and to many a devout reader: how comes it that in this visible Church on earth are so many unworthy members? On purging he says the reference is general, but there was a special thought for Timothy, that if he would separate from all that was evil in his Church at Ephesus then would he indeed be one of those golden vessels unto honour; the image of the great house and its many and varied vessels, though still not quite lost sight of, is passing out of sight, and the verse changes into a note of direct exhortation, since the good and faithful must separate themselves from the evil and faithless, the thought of those deniers of the resurrection of the body being uppermost in St Paul's mind. Robertson says howbeit is a strong adversative, firm an old adjective meaning solid or compact, and knoweth a timeless aorist, the clause being a quotation from Numbers; let every one depart is a paraphrase of Numbers again, and of Isaiah and Jeremiah, the second aorist active imperative being used intransitively, so that it means let every one stand off from, and the whole is probably another echo of the rebellion of Korah. In a great house is the metaphor of a palace: he doubtless has the Kingdom of God in mind, but he works out the metaphor of a great house of the rich and mighty, the adjectives for gold, silver, wood and earth being old or late words used sparingly in the New Testament. If a man purge himself shows that Paul drops the metaphor of the house and takes up the individual as one of the vessels, the verb being an old one meaning to cleanse out; sanctified is a perfect passive participle, and meet for the master's use an old verbal adjective meaning useful or usable.

debates: What the firm foundation is: Gill takes it of the faith of God's elect or of the doctrine of the resurrection, Henry of God's promise or of the truth itself, Clarke of the religion of Christ as a noble mansion, Wesley of God's truth and faithfulness, and Barnes and Ellicott of the Church, which Ellicott calls only the ground-storey of a Temple to be completed in heaven

Whether the great house is the Church or the world: Chrysostom insists that Paul speaks not of the Church only but of the world at large, and warns his hearers plainly not to think he means the Church, while Gill denies the world reading by name and Clarke, Barnes, Ellicott, Robertson and Wesley all take it of the Church

What the seal is: Clarke offers first an inscription over a temple door, comparing Delphi, the mosques and the high priest's mitre, then prefers a contract sealed by two parties, so that the two sentences stand on two seals rather than two faces of one; Ellicott and Henry keep one seal with a motto on each side

Where the sentences come from: Robertson traces both to the rebellion of Korah, the first a quotation and the second a paraphrase of Numbers with Isaiah and Jeremiah, where Ellicott finds the second rather in the command to those that bear the vessels of the Lord to touch no unclean thing
outliers: Clarke's report that he has seen many Asiatic seals bearing no image but only an inscription, and that several lie before him as he writes
Clarke's confession that the apostle has not made the application of these similes and that it is very difficult to tell what he means
Clarke's note that almost all the important manuscripts read Lord rather than Christ
Ellicott's reading of the Church on earth as the first storey of a building the Divine Architect will complete in heaven
Ellicott's paraphrase, that he knows his own because he loves them
Robertson's judgment that the whole verse is another echo of the rebellion of Korah
Wesley's qualification that a vessel even of gold may be put to the vilest use, though that was not the design of him who made it

22.pericope_label: Flee youthful lusts, and instruct opposers in meekness

schools.summary: Gill says the youthful lusts meant are not lusts of uncleanness, lasciviousness and filthiness, nor any of those follies and vanities which the youthful age usually lusts after, to which Timothy was not inclined, but such lusts as are apt to prevail with young ministers of the Gospel, such as vain glory, popular applause, seeking to have the pre-eminence, contentions with and contempt of others, and the like. Foolish and unlearned questions are such as have no solid wisdom in them and are foreign from the Gospel, the wisdom of God in a mystery, and are not useful and unedifying; such ought to be avoided publicly and privately, and should not be started in the public ministry nor attended to in private conversation, as being unworthy of the notice of a minister of the Gospel who is wise and learned, and useless to the church and to his hearers. By the servant of the Lord, Gill says, is not meant any believer in common but a minister of the word, as Timothy was, and such an one ought not to strive about words to no profit, about mere words, in a litigious, quarrelsome manner, and for mastery and not truth; though he may and ought to strive for the faith of the Gospel, and this is praiseworthy in him. Those that oppose themselves oppose the truth, resist it and deny it, or contradict some other tenets and principles of theirs, or the Scriptures which they themselves allowed to be the word of God and the rule of faith and practice, and so are self-convinced and self-condemned; these are to be instructed, being ignorant, and in a tender and gentle manner, though very perverse and obstinate. That they may recover themselves means that they may awake and come to themselves and appear to be sober and in their right mind, the metaphor being taken from drunken men who are overcharged and not in their senses, and being stupefied fall asleep; and like these are persons intoxicated with errors and heresies, who when their minds are enlightened and they are convinced of their evil tenets repent of them, come to themselves and acknowledge the truth.

Henry says Paul here exhorts Timothy to beware of youthful lusts, and that though he was a holy good man, very much mortified to the world, Paul still thought it necessary to caution him against them: flee them, take all possible care and pains to keep thyself pure from them. The lusts of the flesh are youthful lusts, which young people must carefully watch against, and the best must not be secure; and Paul prescribes an excellent remedy against them, to follow righteousness, faith, charity and peace. Youthful lusts are very dangerous, Henry observes, for which reason even hopeful young people have need to be warned of them.

Clarke says the youthful lusts are not only all irregular and sensual desires, but pride, ambition, and above all the lust of power, to which most men will sacrifice all other propensities, their ease, pleasure, health and the rest; this is the most bewitching passion in the human heart, and both in Church and state it is ruinous, but particularly so in the former. Timothy was now between thirty and forty years of age, the very age in which ambition and the love of power most generally prevail: carnal pleasures are the sins of youth, ambition and the love of power the sins of middle age, and covetousness and carking cares the crimes of old age. To follow righteousness is to flee from sin and pursue goodness. Of the opposers he says the word seems to refer to those who opposed the apostle's authority, and hence the propriety of the allusion to the rebellion of Korah and his company; the minister was to use every means which he had reason to believe God might bless, and the apostle intimates that, bad as they were, they were not out of the reach of God's mercy. Of the last verse Clarke says the construction is extremely difficult, though the sense given by our translation is plain enough, and he sets down the original together with the principal English translations, from Wiclif's of the fourteenth century and Coverdale's first printed English Bible of the sixteenth, to show how variously it has been rendered. His own conclusion is that those who had risen up against the authority of St Paul, chief among them Hymeneus and Philetus, would be dealt with by God as he dealt with Korah, Dathan and Abiram and their company; and as the true Israelites were to separate themselves from the tents of those wicked men, so Timothy and the believers at Ephesus were to hold no sort of communion with those workers of iniquity. This subject, Clarke says, the apostle further illustrates by a contract between two parties, each of which sets his seal to the instrument, the seal bearing the motto peculiar to the party; this he conceives to be the meaning, but the common mode of interpretation will, it is probable, be most commonly followed. Wesley says the desires are those peculiarly incident to youth, that the peace to be followed is unity with all true believers, and that youthful desires destroy the purity of heart which righteousness, faith, love and peace accompany. A servant of the Lord must not strive eagerly or passionately, as do the vain wranglers spoken of, but be apt to teach, chiefly by patience and unwearied assiduity. In meekness, Wesley says, he has often need of zeal, always of meekness; and if haply God should give them repentance, it is wholly his work, the acknowledging of the truth quickly following. Those spoken of at the last are at present not only captives but asleep, utterly insensible of their captivity.

Barnes says Paul felt that Timothy, then a young man, was subject to the same passions as other young men, and hence his repeated cautions to him to avoid all those things arising from his youth which might be the occasion of scandal; it is to be remembered, he adds, that this epistle is applicable to other ministers as well as to Timothy, and that to a young man in the ministry no counsel could be more appropriate. Of the questions he says the word rendered unlearned means trifling, that which does not tend to edification, stupid; the Greeks and the Hebrews were greatly given to controversies of various kinds, and many of the questions discussed pertained to points which could not be settled, or which, if settled, were of no importance, such having been the character of no small part of the disputes which have agitated the world, and Paul correctly says that the only effect of such disputes is to engender harsh contention. The servant of the Lord refers here primarily to the Christian minister but is applicable to all Christians, since all profess to be the servants of the Lord; he may calmly inquire after truth, may discuss points of morals or theology if he will do it with a proper spirit, and may contend earnestly for the faith once delivered to the saints, but he may not do what is here mentioned as strife, the Greek word commonly denoting to fight, to make war, to contend. On instructing those that oppose themselves, that is, those who embrace error and array themselves against the truth, Barnes says we are not to become angry with such persons and denounce them at once as heretics, nor to hold them up to public reproach and scorn, but to set about the business of patiently instructing them: their grand difficulty, it is supposed in this direction, is that they are ignorant of the truth, and our business with them is calmly to show them what the truth is; if they are angry we are not to be, and if they oppose the truth we are still calmly to state it to them. Of the recovery he says the word occurs nowhere else in the New Testament and properly means to become sober again, as from inebriation, to awake from a deep sleep, and then to come to a right mind as one does who is aroused from a state of inebriety or from sleep; the representation implies that while under the influence of error they were like a man intoxicated, or like one in deep slumber, and from this state they were to be roused. Ellicott says he who would indeed become a vessel for honour in that great house of God must do more than merely separate himself from all outward communion and friendship with men who by their teaching and in their lives did dishonour to the Master's religion: there was an inner work to be accomplished as well as an outer and more public protest to be made, and he must fight with and conquer those lusts, passions and desires which are more peculiarly tempting to those who are still in the meridian of life, since that Timothy was not now in early manhood has already been shown. The Greek word translated unlearned is better rendered ignorant, since these questions, which the false teachers with whom Timothy was so much thrown loved to put forward for discussion, could hardly be termed unlearned, much useless learning being often thrown away in these disputings of the schools, but were rather pointless and stupid as well as foolish. Although these directions belong in all cases to God's servants of every degree and calling, Ellicott says, yet some of them peculiarly apply to Timothy and those like him specially devoted to the ministry of the Word; and so here everything likely to be the cause of strife, heart-burning or hot words is singularly out of place in the life of a servant of that Lord who fulfilled to the letter the Isaiah prophecy of Messiah, that he shall not strive nor cry. By those that oppose themselves St Paul alludes scarcely so much to the leading teachers of false doctrine as to those led away by them: in the Epistle to Titus we read how the pronounced heretics, no doubt the teachers and leaders of the school, were after a first and second admonition to be shunned and left to themselves, whereas these were evidently to be dealt with in a different manner, their treatment to be a gentle one, nothing being said here respecting a first and second admonition only and no hint given that these are to be shunned. The literal meaning of the Greek word rendered that they may recover themselves is that they may awake from drunkenness, though the English version gives the meaning with great exactness: those taken in the snare of the devil are represented as not only captives in that snare but also as helplessly wrapped in slumber, and the deadly peril of all captives of sin is here well painted, since these unhappy ones, before they can free themselves from the toils of the evil one, must awake from the deep slumber in which they are wrapped. Of the closing words Ellicott notes that the first pronoun, referred here to the devil, and the second, referred here to God, are represented in the Greek by two distinct words. Robertson says youthful is a literary word found in Polybius and Josephus and only here in the New Testament, there being lusts peculiar to flaming youth; flee is a present active imperative, and follow after is used as if in a chase, a steady pursuit of these virtues. Ignorant is an old verbal found only here in the New Testament, meaning untrained or uneducated, which Parry renders the speculations of a half-educated mind; refuse is the same word used in First Timothy, and they gender strifes means, in the present active indicative of an old and common verb, they beget battles. Must not strive is rather, it is not necessary for him to fight in such verbal quibbles, the negative going with the verb of obligation and not with the infinitive; gentle is an old word from the word for speech, meaning affable or mild, found in the New Testament only here; teachable is the word of First Timothy, and forbearing a late compound meaning putting up with evil, found only here. Correcting is the word for schooling; oppose themselves is the present middle participle of a late double compound found in Diodorus and Philo, meaning to place oneself in opposition, and found only here in the New Testament; and the clause about God giving repentance uses a rare late form of the second aorist active optative. They may recover themselves is the first aorist active subjunctive of a late and rare word meaning to be sober again, found only here in the New Testament: they have been caught while mentally intoxicated in the devil's snare. Taken captive is the perfect passive participle of an old verb meaning to take alive, found in the New Testament only here and in Luke of Peter, so that it means taken captive alive; and the difficult phrase that follows, Robertson says, is understood variously.

debates: Which lusts are meant: Clarke takes them of pride, ambition and above all the lust of power, dating Timothy between thirty and forty and assigning carnal pleasures to youth, ambition to middle age and covetousness to old age; Gill narrows them to the lusts of young ministers, vain glory and popular applause and pre-eminence, denying Timothy was inclined to the others; Henry keeps the plainer sense of fleshly lusts

What is wrong with the questions: Ellicott says unlearned is better rendered ignorant, since much useless learning is thrown away in the disputings of the schools and the fault is pointlessness rather than want of learning, where Barnes takes the word as trifling and stupid and blames the subject matter, points which could not be settled or which if settled were of no importance

Who the opposers are: Ellicott holds they are not the leading teachers, since the pronounced heretics of Titus were to be shunned after two admonitions whereas nothing of the kind is said here, but rather those led away by them; Clarke takes them as those who opposed the apostle's own authority, which is why the chapter alludes to the rebellion of Korah

What the last verse means: Clarke calls the construction extremely difficult, prints the Greek beside the older English versions to show the disagreement, and offers his own reading of a two-party contract with the Korah warning behind it, while Ellicott settles the pronouns by their being two distinct Greek words, the first of the devil and the second of God, and Robertson says only that the phrase is understood variously
